method: The gain computer works in decibels. Above the threshold the output rises 1 dB for every R dB of input, where R is the ratio, so a 4:1 setting turns 4 dB over the threshold into 1 dB over it; the gain reduction is (input - threshold) x (1 / R - 1), which is zero at the threshold and more negative as the input climbs, and the output level is the input plus that reduction. A ratio of 1:1 gives no reduction at all, while a very high ratio approaches limiting at the threshold without ever being treated as one. Below the threshold the reduction is zero and the signal passes unchanged. A soft knee of width W is centred on the threshold: across the interval from threshold - W/2 to threshold + W/2 the reduction follows slope x (over + W/2)^2 / (2 W), which is zero at the lower edge, a quarter of the knee's full reduction at the threshold and exactly the hard-knee value at the upper edge, so the curve and its slope join smoothly at both ends. Makeup gain is added after the gain computer and the peak-restoring figure is the negative of the gain reduction. Threshold and input level are limited to -80 to 0 dBFS, ratio to 1 to 40, knee width to 0 to 24 dB and makeup gain to 0 to 36 dB; blank fields, exponent notation and text are refused with the reason, and results carry two decimals with negative zero normalised. The model is the static transfer curve at one peak level: attack and release timing, programme-dependent behaviour, RMS or loudness detection, look-ahead, sidechain filtering and parallel mix are not modelled, so a real compressor on music moves around these figures. Everything is calculated in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.
